doc.title: Aebersold Jamey — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The first Play-A-Long record in 1967
summary: He shows the first Play-A-Long, sold from his car trunk, on consignment and by a DownBeat ad, recorded in a Bloomington music store.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: This is actually the very first one, because there’s no ad or anything on the back. No real cover. Just paper.
Let me zoom in just a little bit here.
You tell me when we’re going.

Yeah. This is the very first Play-A-Long record, which came out in 1967. No ad on the back. The drawing was done by my sister-in-law. Handwritten music, not done on Finale. Scales and exercises, a little blues, a little of this-that-and-the-other. Interesting. “A new approach to jazz improvisation.”
So ’67 is really when commercially you started to...
And how did you go about... Because we were talking about now the marketing approach is a little different. Was this when you went to camps you brought it along and sold it, and....
Sold them out of the trunk of the car, with an LP, so to speak.

Yes. But I took it also to some music stores in Louisville, on consignment, and was so delighted when I’d go back a month or six weeks later, and they would have sold 2 or 3. And then I put an ad in DownBeat, a little-bitty classified.
Recording-wise, where did you go? What studio? Or how did you go about recording?

We recorded it up at Bloomington, at a music store downtown, right next to the railroad tracks, because they had a grand piano. We had to stop once or twice because the train went through. Then we’ve re-recorded it several times since then, because recording standards got higher and so forth.
So when somebody orders this, you don’t send out the first recording of it? That’s more of just out the hole and historical...
Yeah. And a couple of people have put them on CDs for me and sent me copies of them.
